source.title: Towards a Comprehensive Scaling Law of Mixture-of-Experts
source.authors: Guoliang Zhao; Yu-Han Fu; Shuai-Peng Li; Xing-Wu Sun; Ruo-Bing Xie; An Wang; Wei-Dong Han; Zhen Yang; Wei-Xuan Sun; Yudong Zhang; Cheng-Zhong Xu; Di Wang; Jie Jiang

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. Some equations and tables show minor text-extraction/layout artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling in MoE language models and refines the claim for that setting: it finds power-law-like effects for total parameters and data, but non-monotonic effects for several MoE-specific factors, and proposes a multi-factor loss law.
record.gate_note: Rows record the paper's own marginal experiments, fitting comparisons and larger-scale validation. Cited results from other studies are excluded. The optimal G, S and activated-parameter-ratio recommendations are not rows because they do not test the listed versions. The fixed-compute analysis varies activated parameters and data at fixed total model size; it does not test the parameter/token allocation claim in V3.
record.test_reason: The study trains 446 MoE language models on Dolma. It checks whether loss follows power laws in total parameters N and tokens D, and fits a joint law that it validates on larger runs. It argues the dense Chinchilla form is insufficient for MoE and restates it with Na, G and S terms. Ranges are modest: N 133M–3.4B for fitting and up to 9B for validation; D 10B–50B for fitting and up to 100B for validation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also argue that dense scaling laws are inapplicable to MoE. From the fitted law they conclude that optimal G (about 7) and S (about 0.31) are independent of size and data, and that the optimal Na/N ratio becomes sparser as N grows.
record.recipe_differences: This is a MoE-specific study, not a reproduction of the dense-model scaling-law experiments. It conducts 446 controlled experiments, fits a joint law over five factors, and evaluates it against MoE experiment data.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported loss relationships vary with MoE-specific factors Na, G and S; the paper also says the S trend becomes more prominent with larger model size and the G trend is affected by data/model settings.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed N=1T, G=7 and S=0.31, the fitted law implies optimal loss L*(C)≈1.87+576·C^-0.158 with C=D·Na.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For fixed total MoE size, the optimal loss against activated compute follows a derived power law.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted law gives an optimal G≈6.78 and S≈0.31, independent of N, Na and D, and an optimal Na/N that falls as N grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MoE models the optimal expert granularity and shared ratio are scale-invariant, and optimal sparsity increases with total size.

record.problems: The reported experiments cover N up to 3.4B for fitting and 9B for validation, and the paper notes that it has not validated the law at extremely larger scales or on alternative MoE architectures and training objectives. Validation is on the study's own experiment settings. No uncertainty estimates for the reported fit errors or marginal relationships are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted. Individual experiment configurations and figure points are represented by aggregate rows where the paper reports aggregate trends or fit errors.

untested.parts: Dense models. Scaling over several orders of magnitude (D spans <1 order, N about 1.4). Compute as the scaling variable.
Extrapolation by orders of magnitude; the tested range is only 2–3x beyond the fit range.
Not tested: there is no compute-optimal N versus D allocation; the fixed-compute analysis fixes total N.
Depth and width at fixed parameter count; only the MoE expert settings G and S are varied.
Not tested: no other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Whether published exponents or compute-optimal splits shift with setup or fitting choices.

missing.what: Fitted joint-law exponents α≈0.2383 for N/Na and β≈0.4694 for D, useful for comparing against dense-law exponents.
Larger-model checks of the G, S and Na/N marginal curves at N=3.96B and 7.25B.
Size of the loss change across G at fixed N and Na (Figs 3 and 11), needed to judge V4 for G.

record.verdict_notes: Fit-error comparisons against the paper's own nested forms and refitted baselines (R7, R8, R10, R11) are method comparisons and should not carry version links. G and S at fixed N and Na are architecture-shape variables, so they bear on V4 rather than V7. No uncertainty estimates are given. Preprint.

versions.untested_parts: Tests total model size and data size in MoE models, and activated model size in controlled settings. Does not test dense models, compute scaling, or the full range of language-model pretraining setups.

Tests validation against larger MoE models and data, but not extrapolation by orders of magnitude: the reported ranges extend to 9B total parameters and 100B tokens, versus fitting ranges up to 3.4B and 50B tokens.

The fixed-compute analysis holds total model size fixed and examines activated model size and data; it does not test how loss-minimising total parameter and token counts separately scale with compute.
Does not compare depth, width or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests classical MoE language-model pretraining, not other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.

Shows nonlinear or non-monotonic MoE-factor relationships and compares fitting forms on the same data. It does not test whether published exponents or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations change with setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: MoE models
rows.operation_detail: Varied total model size N while holding G, S, D and Na unchanged; measured validation loss.

conditions.value: G, S, D and Na held unchanged

rows.measure: Validation loss versus total model size N
rows.value: The paper reports a distinct power-law relationship; log validation loss and log N show a linear relationship across the tested model-size ranges.
rows.note: The paper describes this as a marginal relationship in controlled MoE experiments.
rows.check: Link is correct. N spans only about 1.4 orders of magnitude (133M–3.4B). The paper gives no per-sweep fit statistic; the exponent α≈0.238 comes from the joint fit (Table 2).

rows.subject: MoE models
rows.operation_detail: Varied training data size D while holding the other factors fixed; measured validation loss.
rows.measure: Validation loss versus data size D
rows.value: The paper reports a significant power-law relationship; log validation loss and log D show a linear relationship.
rows.note: The paper also reports that groups with the same model size and different data sizes translate along the y-axis.
rows.check: Link is correct. D spans only 10B–50B, under one order of magnitude, so this supports the power-law form only over a narrow range. Joint-fit β≈0.469 (Table 2).

rows.subject: MoE models
rows.size_stated: N ∈ [133M, 3.4B] in fitting experiments; controlled examples include N = 247M, 496M, 907M and 2.4B
rows.operation_detail: Varied activated model size Na while keeping total model size N fixed, by changing expert dimension and routed-expert count.
rows.measure: Validation loss versus activated model size Na
rows.value: At small Na/N the relationship is described as power-law-like; as Na/N increases, loss tends to rise, producing an overall hook-like pattern.
rows.note: The paper attributes the rise at larger Na/N to structural distortion as expert size grows and the number of experts falls.
rows.check: Remove V1. Na is varied at fixed total N by trading expert size against expert count, so this is a structural change at fixed parameter count, not parameter scaling. It does bear on V7: loss versus activated parameters bends into a hook rather than following one power law.

rows.subject: MoE models
rows.size_stated: Controlled settings include Na/N pairs 48M/246M, 99M/495M and 181M/907M
rows.operation_detail: Varied number of activated experts G while holding other factors constant.

conditions.value: controlled; additional S=0 experiments appear in Figure 11

rows.value: Validation loss first decreases and then increases with G; the paper models the marginal relationship with a hook function.
rows.note: The paper says the exponent term for G approaches 1 and omits it in the joint law.
rows.check: Re-link from V7 to V4. Varying G at fixed N and Na is an architecture change at a fixed parameter count. G is not a scale variable, so a G hook says nothing about power-law bending (V7). The text gives no size of the loss differences across G, so the state cannot be read.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3; Equation 8; Figures 3 and 11; Appendix C.4

rows.subject: MoE models
rows.operation_detail: Varied shared-expert ratio S while holding other factors fixed.
rows.measure: Validation loss versus shared-expert ratio S
rows.value: The paper states that models with shared experts significantly outperform those without them; loss first decreases and then increases as S rises, with relatively minor loss impact around the optimum.
rows.note: The paper reports that the S relationship becomes more prominent as model size grows.
rows.check: Re-link from V7 to V4; S is an architecture detail at fixed N and Na. Figure 14 loss ranges across S=0–0.7 are only 0.0014 (247M) to 0.0181 (3.96B), small despite the paper's wording that shared experts 'significantly outperform'.
